payload.goal: Bind every commit to the initiative that produced it, exactly and at commit time, and spend that primitive on two gaps that share it. Gap 1 (staleness): several initiatives share one worktree and one branch, so any session's push carries other initiatives' commits and their records never learn their work shipped. Gap 2 (review): closing an initiative is today an unconditional append — nothing rechecks that the execution was right, and a reviewer with no diff can only re-read the record's own prose and confirm it. The design split that makes both reliable: RECORD commit-to-initiative (append-only, can never go stale, since a commit's initiative never changes) and DERIVE pushed/merged from git at read time (git is truth for git state; the log is truth for intent).

tasks.title: DECIDE the capture mechanism, the crux of the whole initiative. A git post-commit hook catches every commit regardless of author, but sofar installing git hooks is invasive and a terminal commit has no session to attribute to. Judge on what fraction of commits each actually catches, not on elegance; the whole design rests on this being reliable. Log a Decision.

Resolve the record-hygiene D1 collision: git and sofar commands are exempt from the record today, and 1.1 needs `git commit` recorded. Carving it out AMENDS a prior decision — log a Decision that cites D1 explicitly, never a quiet edit to the exemption.

DECIDE what an unattributed commit does (bare terminal, no session, no pin). It must be VISIBLE, never guessed: attributing by file overlap or timestamp produces confident wrong claims, and a wrong "your work shipped" is worse than a silent gap. Pick the surface (doctor finding, digest line, or both).

Back-compat probe, the initiative-lifecycle 1.1 discipline: verify EMPIRICALLY against a published older engine what it does with a commit-attribution event it does not know. Expected: skipped with a warning, degrading safe. Confirm or refute BEFORE designing on top of it.

Event type + payload, in packages/schema/src/ ONLY. Carries the sha; carries NO pushed/merged field — those are derived, never recorded (see the record/derive split in the goal). Deciding the payload is deciding what can never go stale.

Capture at commit time per 1.1, and verify the recorded sha is the commit THIS session just made. Concurrent sessions share this worktree, so a naive `git rev-parse HEAD` after the fact can pick up a peer's commit — prove the race is closed, do not assume it.

doctor: commits reachable on the branch that are attributed to NO initiative — 1.3's surface, and the reconciliation path for anything the capture mechanism missed.

Derive pushed/merged at read time with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> <remote ref>` — never record it, since a force-push or rebase would strand a recorded fact instantly. Decide the behaviour when the remote ref is stale, absent, or never fetched: say "unknown", never guess "unpushed".

Digest surface: replace the weak "N events since write-back" staleness hint with the real signal — "N of this initiative's commits reached origin/main via another session's push". This is the payoff the whole initiative is for. Must stay inside the ≤10,000-char SessionStart guarantee.

DECIDE whether PR state is in scope at all. It is the one piece needing `gh` and a network call, and "no sync service" is a guard-rail in CLAUDE.md. Default is OUT until a Decision says otherwise; pushed/merged already carries most of the staleness value without leaving the machine.

DECIDE review granularity and who pays. Phase boundaries fit a session (3-5 tasks, warm memory, cheap fixes); close-only asks one session to audit 25 tasks at maximum surface and coldest memory. The evidence packet, rendered from the record (a projection — templates dir only): the phase's commit range and diff from Phase 2's attribution, the tasks claimed done, the decisions IN FORCE when that work happened, the rejected approaches, and any guard violations. The verdict event: what was found, what is still open, and whether surviving findings become tasks in the plan. A review that can only ever emit "looks good" is a rubber stamp — the verdict must be able to be "no".

Keep review DECOUPLED from marking done. If passing the review is what lets a session go home, the reviewing agent has an incentive to pass and will find nothing. Review emits findings; close reads them; they are separate steps.

payload.because: The range design is a heuristic, and its two failure modes are fatal to gap 1. Critically, git hooks INHERIT it — a probe prepare-commit-msg hook wrote the live session id into a commit message. payload.because: Measured on this repo (454 commits, 20 iterations, median): `git rev-parse HEAD` — a trivial command doing no work — costs 8.35ms, which is essentially pure process spawn. A bounded 20-commit trailer walk is 10.35ms, last-100 is 15.55ms, and the full walk is 21.21ms with a 45.25ms tail. The shim budget is 100ms and record-integrity D13 measured 63-67ms already spent, leaving ~33ms — so the full walk's tail alone would blow it, and even the cheapest possible git subprocess eats a quarter of the headroom before doing anything useful. That is precisely why core/git.ts is subprocess-free, and the rule holds. The saving grace is that the expensive answer only changes when a ref moves, and detecting THAT is free by the existing file-based ref read: cheap check on the hot path, expensive walk only on actual change, which is rare. Bounding every walk is what makes it scale — spawn cost is fixed, but a full walk is O(history) and would grow without limit on a large repo, while `origin..HEAD` and `-n k` stay flat. In-process object parsing was rejected: loose objects are inflatable but packed history is not, so it would solve the small case and fail the real one.
payload.chose: 2.2: the trailer read is a BOUNDED `git log` subprocess that never runs unconditionally on the hot hook path. The hot path keeps doing what readGitState already does — read refs from FILES, no subprocess — and that ref identity is the cache key. The walk is paid only when a ref actually moved (a commit or a push), or on demand from a CLI command. Every walk is bounded (`origin/<branch>..HEAD`, or `-n <k>`), never a full-history walk.
payload.over: Putting a `git log` walk directly on the PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit path the way record-integrity 4.4 put push state there; doing a full-history walk and accepting the cost; and parsing commit objects in-process to avoid the subprocess entirely.
payload.rule: Never run a git subprocess unconditionally on the hot hook path, and never walk full history — bound every walk, and gate it on a ref actually having moved.

Why it is worth obeying rather than shipping incrementally. Attribution is a CHAIN — the prepare-commit-msg hook writes the trailer, core/attribution.ts reads it, doctor reports whether it is working, and the shipping notice and review packet consume it. Publishing a partial chain puts users in the worst state available: the hook installs and writes trailers while some consumer is missing, or doctor reports "attribution off" in a version that has no way to turn it on. The current repo state is the honest one BECAUSE nothing is published — the PATH binary is 0.25.1, predates commit-trailer, so the hook is deliberately not installed and doctor says so accurately.

Two consequences for any session working here. First, do not install the prepare-commit-msg hook in this repo before the release; trailers stay hand-written until then, and doctor's accurate "attribution off" is more useful than a misleading "installed but nothing attributed". Second, session-orientation's protocol-block change rides the same release — protocol blocks are a versioned ledger and a half-shipped one leaves repos matching no known version, so that initiative's Phase 1 is part of what must land before publishing.

Publishing itself remains the user's action (they run `npm publish -w sofar.sh` for the classifier and OTP), so this gate is about not ASKING for it early, not about permission.

payload.because: The caveat was survivable only because this repo commits straight to main — it becomes the normal case the first time work lands through a squashed PR, and it fails in the direction that matters: shipped work reads as un-shipped, so 3.2 and 3.4 would keep telling a session to push work that had already landed. Recovering the slug is still READING git, which is the line D4 draws, because the text is present verbatim in the object; nothing is inferred from timestamps or file overlap. The two gates are what keep it from degrading into a guess: running only on an empty trailer block means a properly attributed commit can never be re-labelled by its own prose (this very repo commits messages that quote the trailer key), and requiring indentation means it reads the shape a squash actually produces rather than every mention of the key — an unindented one at the end of a message is already a trailer and git has parsed it. Rewriting SQUASH_MSG at write time was rejected as the wrong layer: it would only help squashes performed on a machine with the hook installed, while the read side has to work on any clone, and D7 already refuses to own more of the user's git surface than it must. The `-m` case stays honestly unattributed and that is not a gap to close later — committing a squash with `-m` discards SQUASH_MSG entirely, so the slug is not in the object at all and inventing one is exactly what D5 forbids.

payload.rule: Recover a squashed slug only from an INDENTED body trailer and only when git's trailer block is empty — never let body text override a real trailer, and never invent attribution the commit object does not carry.
